content: Tarragon, also known as dragon's-wort (Artemisia dracunculus L.), is a perennial herb belonging to the Asteraceae family, which is closely related to wormwood. Its species name gives rise to the common nickname dragon herb. This plant is native to a vast region of the Northern Hemisphere, spanning from easternmost Europe through central and eastern Asia to western North America, and extending southward to northern India and Mexico. However, the populations found in North America may have been naturalized following early human introduction. Tarragon typically grows to a height of 120–150 cm, with slender, branched stems. Its leaves are lanceolate in shape, measuring 2–8 cm in length and 2–10 mm in width, and are characterized by a glossy green appearance with smooth, entire margins. The flowers are small, produced in capitula measuring 2–4 mm in diameter, with each capitulum containing up to 40 florets that are yellow or greenish-yellow in color. Cultivation and Uses Tarragon possesses a distinctive aromatic quality reminiscent of anise, which is attributed to the presence of estragole. Among its varieties, French tarragon is widely regarded as the most suitable for culinary purposes, though it cannot be propagated from seed. In contrast, Russian tarragon (Artemisia dracunculoides L.) can be grown from seed but is significantly milder in flavor. Despite its weaker taste, Russian tarragon is a hardier and more vigorous plant, capable of spreading via its roots and growing over a meter tall. It thrives in poor soils and is highly tolerant of drought and neglect. While it lacks the strong aroma and flavor of French tarragon, it produces an abundance of leaves from early spring onward, which are mild and suitable for use in salads and cooked dishes. Additionally, the young stems of Russian tarragon can be cooked as a substitute for asparagus in early spring. Tarragon can be cultivated indoors from seed and transplanted outdoors during the summer. Its spreading nature allows for easy division of the plant. Tarragon is one of the four fines herbes essential to French cuisine and is particularly well-suited for dishes involving chicken, fish, and eggs. It is also a key ingredient in Béarnaise sauce. In some countries, such as Armenia, Georgia, and Russia, tarragon is used to flavor a popular carbonated soft drink known as Tarkhun. This beverage, named after the Armenian, Persian, and Russian word for tarragon, is made from a sugary tarragon concentrate and is brightly colored green. James Beard, a renowned culinary expert, once remarked, I believe that if ever I had to practice cannibalism, I might manage if there were enough tarragon around. From a chemical perspective, cis-pellitorin, an isobutylamide compound known for its pungent taste, has been isolated from the tarragon plant.
